title: The Civilized Mind

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The book unifies several originally independent manuscripts around one diagnosis: humanity’s expanding knowledge and transformative power are outrunning its capacity for honest self-correction. Political polarization, institutional distrust, elite hypocrisy, technological concentration, demographic anxiety, and cultural conflict appear here as expressions of a deeper failure of mind. People and institutions protect moral identities, advantages, and comforting narratives even when reality contradicts them. The civilized mind is therefore not defined by education, refinement, ideological moderation, or possession of correct opinions. It is a practiced ability to seek truth without cruelty, acknowledge difference without converting it into superiority, exercise authority without imagining oneself infallible, and remain open to correction when cherished models fail. The opening argument treats truth as more than accurate information. A difficult truth may threaten dignity, belonging, status, income, innocence, or an entire account of the self; resistance can therefore be psychologically intelligible even when it is factually indefensible. Effective truth is disciplined by purpose, timing, proportion, and care. Speakers should distinguish observation from interpretation, describe conduct rather than condemn identity, confess uncertainty, and ask what repair they want their words to make possible. This is not an instruction to dilute reality or avoid conflict. Silence accumulates resentment, protects profitable blindness, and can make an eventual explosion inevitable. sourceEvidence.locator: Taboo feeds the politics of partial truth
sourceEvidence.excerpt: The work argues that democracies become vulnerable when morally dangerous subjects—fertility, migration, sex, biology, religion, crime, class, cultural norms, elite reproduction, or AI displacement—cannot be discussed without social excommunication. Suppression does not remove the underlying fears; it leaves them available to extremists who combine a neglected observation with a totalizing explanation and an enemy. Yet the book does not assume every taboo conceals wisdom or that every side deserves equal validation. Its method is to recover whatever limited truth a movement has stolen while rejecting the dehumanizing conclusion built upon it. Culture wars intensify through humiliation, status loss, sacred values, envy, distrust of knowledge-producing institutions, competitive victimhood, and platforms that monetize contempt. Across its most controversial terrain, the book attempts to keep empirical or plausible claims separate from moral hierarchy. Biology, sex, temperament, inherited capacity, fertility, demographic change, assortative mating, and cultural transmission may affect societies, it argues, but none makes dignity conditional on competitiveness or turns population groups into destinies. Culture shapes trust, learning, violence, family life, and institutional performance, yet culture is learned, mixed, revised, and escapable rather than reducible to blood. Similarly, unequal ability does not justify caste, while denying meaningful differences can force people through one narrow status competition and humiliate those it predictably excludes.
